sections.title: Escherichia coli is engineered to grow on ${ \mathsf { C O } } _ { 2 }$ and formic acid
sections.content:
Junho Bang  1,2, Chang Hun Hwang  1,2, Jung Ho Ahn1,2, Jong An Lee1,2 and Sang Yup Lee  1,2,3<sup> ✉</sup>

We engineered Escherichia coli to grow on $\mathbf { c o } _ { 2 }$ and formic acid alone by introducing the synthetic $\mathbf { c o } _ { 2 }$ and formic acid assimilation pathway, expressing two formate dehydrogenase genes, fine-tuning metabolic fluxes and optimizing the levels of cytochrome bo and bd-I ubiquinol oxidase. Our engineered strain can grow to an optical density at 600 nm of 7.38 in 450 h, and shows promise as a platform strain growing on $\mathbf { c o } _ { 2 }$ and formic acid alone.

Biological conversion of $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ into useful compounds could enable production of value-added products from CO (ref. 1). To efficiently assimilate $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 } ,$ the combined use of $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and formic acid (FA), which is produced by liquefaction of $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ by a chemical reaction, has been suggested $2 - { 5 }$ FA can be readily produced from $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ (ref. 6), and is easy to store and transport7. FA can be assimilated more efficiently than $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ by microorganisms8 and can be converted into reducing power by formate dehydrogenase (Fdh). Owing to these advantages, development of a synthetic microorganism capable of growing on $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and FA alone has been pursued. Recently, limited growth of Escherichia coli strains on $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and FA has been reported9–11 (Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Note 2). However, the final optical densities at 600 nm $\left( \mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 } \right)$ reached by these engineered E. coli strains was low (up to $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 1). Development of an E. coli strain that can efficiently grow to a higher cell density on $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and FA alone is needed for industrial biotechnology applications.

We engineered an E. coli strain capable of growing on CO and FA alone (Fig. 1a). First, strain FC1 was constructed by introducing a reconstructed tetrahydrofolate (THF) cycle, reverse glycine cleavage reaction and Candida boidinii Fdh (CbFdh) into the E. coli DH5α\_ GTPS strain (a strain with the gcvR, pflB and serA genes deleted and the native promoter of gcvT replaced with trc; Supplementary Note 3, Extended Data Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 2). However, FC1 failed to grow on CO and FA alone (Fig. 1b).

We hypothesized that insufficient gluconeogenesis, simultaneous expression of the purT and ftl genes, and inefficient NADPH supply might be the reasons for the inability of the FC1 strain to grow solely on CO and FA. We solved all three potential problems in turn, resulting in strains FC2 (ppsA overexpression and ppsR deletion in FC1), FC3 (purT deletion in FC2) and FC5 (FC3 strain harbouring p100FA2, which additionally expresses the Arabidopsis thaliana $f d h _ { \mathrm { m u t } }$ gene for NADPH generation from FA; Supplementary Table 2, Supplementary Note 4 and Extended Data Figs. 1b and 2a–d). FC5 grew on $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and FA alone (Fig. 1b and Extended Data Fig. 3a) to an $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 0.285 (0.0633 g dry cell weight (DCW) l−1) in 150 h from an initial $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 0.051 (0.0169 g DCW l−1), showing about 2.5 cell doublings; also, the number of colony-forming units (c.f.u.)

was increased (Extended Data Fig. 3b). Assimilation of $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and FA was confirmed by 13C isotope analysis (Extended Data Fig. 4 and Supplementary Note 5). These results suggest that FC5 can grow on CO and FA alone with active cell division. Next, optimization of isopropyl-β-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG) concentration and aeration conditions enabled cells to grow to a higher density. As a result, the FC5 strain grew to a higher $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 0.533 (from the initial $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 0.07) in 200 h in optimized conditions, which was 0.87-fold higher than that $\left( \mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 } \right)$ of 0.285) obtained earlier (Supplementary Note 6 and Extended Data Fig. 5a–c).

We then optimized plasmid gene expression levels because excessive gene expression might negatively affect cell growth during limited nutrient supply, especially in a medium containing CO and FA alone. Plasmid gene expression levels were fine-tuned by using plasmids with lower copy numbers in FC5 (Fig. 1c) to yield strains FC7 and FC8 (Supplementary Note 7 and Supplementary Table 2), which harboured medium- and low-copy-number plasmids, respectively. The FC8 strain grew up to an $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 0.607 (from the initial $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 0.06) in 200 h solely on $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and FA, 0.14-fold higher than that $( \mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 0.533) of the FC5 strain, while the FC7 strain grew to an $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 0.452, slightly lower than that of the FC5 strain (Fig. 1d). The $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and FA assimilation fluxes and the amount of FA consumed by FC8 were higher than in FC5 (Extended Data Fig. 6a,b), suggesting that in FC5 the plasmid gene expression levels were higher than those actually needed for cell growth on $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and FA (Supplementary Note 7). To demonstrate that the FC8 strain was able to grow to a higher cell density solely on $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and FA, it was cultured using a higher initial inoculum level $( \mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 0.35). The FC8 strain grew to an $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 1.24 (0.343 g DCW l−1) in 100 h (Fig. 2a). Cells were found to be filamented (Fig. 2b), which seems to be one of the reasons for no further growth beyond the $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 1.24 as cell filamentation negatively affects cell growth12.

We hypothesized that cell filamentation might be due to energy deficiency in the cells when growing on CO and FA alone. One way of solving energy deficiency is to more efficiently convert reducing power to ATP. Reducing the cultivation temperature (for example, 28 and $3 3 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ can improve energy efficiency by increasing the expression level of cytochrome bo ubiquinol oxidase (Cyo) while decreasing the expression level of cytochrome bd-I ubiquinol oxidase (Cyd; Fig. 2c and Supplementary Note 8). We monitored growth of FC8 at 30, 32 and ${ \bar { 3 } } { \bar { 3 } } ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ . The highest level of cell growth was observed at $3 2 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ (see Supplementary Note 9 and Extended Data Fig. 7a–c for detailed results); the FC8 strain grew from an initial $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 0.31 to an $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 2.48 (0.687 g DCW l−1) in 244 h (Fig. 2d), consuming 0.41 g FA (for example, $8 . 2 \mathrm { g l } ^ { - 1 }$ FA equivalent). We found that the messenger RNA levels of the cyoAB and cydAB genes, which encode Cyo and Cyd, respectively, were changed as intended at $3 2 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ compared with those at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ (Extended Data Fig. 7d). The biomass yields on FA were $0 . 0 5 5 2 { \scriptstyle \pm 0 . 0 0 0 9 }$ and 0.0365 ± 0.0026 g DCW g−1 FA when the FC8 strain was cultured at 32 and $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { { C } } ,$ respectively (Fig. 2e), suggesting that increasing the Cyo level and decreasing the Cyd level enhanced energy efficiency when growing solely on CO and FA. Thus, cell filamentation was suppressed (Fig. 2b) by more efficiently converting reducing power to ATP.

The red, black, blue and dashed arrows indicate heterologous pathways, native pathways, reinforced native pathways and multiple-step pathways, respectively. The red crosses indicate the deleted genes. b, The growth profiles of the FC1, 2, 3 and 5 strains solely on CO and FA. c, The plasmids constructed to alter the expression levels of the genes associated with the CO and FA assimilation pathway and two Fdhs. d, The growth profiles of the FC7 and 8 strains. We cultivated our optimized FC8 strain in a flask starting with a low initial $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 0.018 to examine the maximum number of cell doublings. FC8 grew to an $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 3.59 (0.994 g DCW l−1) in 791.5 h, consuming 0.94 g FA (for example, $1 8 . 8 \mathrm { g l ^ { - 1 } }$ FA equivalent; Fig. 2f), showing 7.64 doublings. As cells grew, the specific growth rate decreased, and consequently the doubling time increased; the specific growth rates at the initial and final time points were 0.0105 and $0 . 0 0 \bar { 2 } 8 \mathrm { h } ^ { - 1 }$ , respectively, while the doubling times were 65.9 and 250.6 h, respectively (Extended Data Fig. 8a).

To determine the maximum achievable $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 } ,$ a bioreactor culture of FC8 starting with a high initial $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 1.02 was analysed. FC8 grew to a maximum $\mathrm { \ O D } _ { 6 0 0 } ^ { - }$ of 7.38 (2.044 g DCW l−1) from an initial $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 1.02 in $4 5 0 \mathrm { h } ,$ consuming 18.2 g FA (for example, $3 6 . 4 \mathrm { g l ^ { - 1 } }$ FA equivalent; Fig. 2g). Three additional bioreactor cultures were independently performed to examine reproducibility, resulting in the maximum $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 7.88 (2.074 g DCW l−1) from an initial $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 1.15 in 412 h, 8.01 (2.29 g DCW l−1) from an initial $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 1.06 in 412 h, and 11.1 (3.466 g DCW l−1) from an initial $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 0.91 in 577 h, respectively (more detailed results are presented in Supplementary Note 10 and Extended Data Fig. 8b–f); thus, the FC8 strain was able to grow to an $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 7–11 from the initial $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of about 1.

In summary, we engineered an E. coli strain capable of growing on $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and FA alone to a higher cell density than previously reported strains. Our work could enable bio-based production of chemicals solely from $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and FA in future (Supplementary Discussion). Although we developed an engineered strain capable of growing to a higher cell density, the low specific growth rate still needs to be improved. This might be achievable using adaptive laboratory evolution of FC8, further metabolic engineering to increase $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 } / \mathrm { \dot { F } A }$ assimilation and energy generation, and/or optimization of bioreactor cultivation conditions.

Reagents. All chemicals used in this study were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich unless otherwise noted. Q5 High-Fidelity DNA Polymerase from New England Biolabs or Pfu-x DNA Polymerase from Solgent was used for PCR. Each genomic DNA was extracted using a genomic DNA extraction kit from Intron Biotechnology. All PCR products and plasmids were purified and extracted with the PCR purification kit and plasmid extraction kit, respectively, from Intron Biotechnology. All oligonucleotides were purchased from Genotech. DNA sequencing was performed at Macrogen.

The data presented in g represent the result of one bioreactor cultivation; the results of other reproduced bioreactor cultivations are shown in Extended Data Fig. 8d–f.

Bacterial strains and medium composition. The E. coli strains and plasmids used in this study are listed in Supplementary Table 2. E. coli DH5α was used as a gene cloning host and base strain for developing the engineered formatotrophic strain. Lysogeny broth (LB) medium and M9 medium (pH 7.0) were used in this study. The LB medium contains (per litre) 10 g tryptone, 5 g yeast extract and 10 g NaCl. The M9 minimal medium (pH 7.0) contains (per litre) $6 . 8 \mathrm { g N a _ { 2 } H P O _ { 4 } } { \cdot } 7 \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { \ ' O } , 3 \mathrm { g }$ KH PO , 0.5 g NaCl, 2 g NH Cl, 4.2 g NaHCO , 0.8 g MgSO ·7H O, 0.24 g IPTG, 0.05 g ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA), 0.002 g thiamine·HCl and 5 ml trace metal solution. The trace metal solution contains (per litre of 0.5 M HCl) 10 g $\mathrm { F e S O _ { 4 } { \cdot } 7 H _ { 2 } O , 2 g C a C l _ { 2 } , 2 . 2 g Z n S O _ { 4 } { \cdot } 7 H _ { 2 } O , 0 . 5 g }$ MnSO ·4H O, 1 g CuSO ·5H O, $0 . 1 \mathrm { g } ( \mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ) _ { 6 } \mathrm { M o } _ { 7 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 4 } { \cdot } 4 \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ and 0.02 g Na B O ·10H O. The pH of the M9 medium was adjusted using 1 M NaOH solution.

Plasmid construction. Plasmid p100FA1 construction was carried out as follows. The DNA fragment of plasmid backbone was prepared by PCR with 100\_F/ mtd\_R primers using the plasmid p100THF as a template. The DNA fragment of FDHcbo was prepared by PCR with FDHcbo\_F/FDHcbo\_R primers using genomic DNA of C. boidinii as a template. Next, the purified DNA fragments of the plasmid backbone and FDHcbo were ligated by a Gibson assembly reaction following the standard protocol13. Finally, the DNA sequence of the constructed plasmid p100FA1 was confirmed by DNA sequencing. Hereafter, all of the plasmid construction procedures were carried out by following the method described above. The plasmid p100FA2 was constructed by a Gibson assembly reaction using the DNA fragments of plasmid backbone and FDHatmut. These DNA fragments were prepared by PCR with 100\_F/FDHcbo\_R1 primers using p100FA1 as a template and FDHat\_F/FDHat\_R primers using the synthesized FDHatmut DNA fragment as a template, respectively. The plasmid p184FA was constructed by a Gibson assembly reaction using the DNA fragments of plasmid backbone and C1\_OPR. These DNA fragments were prepared by PCR with 184\_F/184\_R primers using pACYC184 as a template and with C1\_F/C1\_R primers using the plasmid p100FA2 as a template, respectively. The plasmid p518FA was constructed by a Gibson assembly reaction using the DNA fragments of plasmid backbone and C1\_OPR. These DNA fragments were prepared by PCR with 518\_F/518\_R primers using pJH518 as a template and with C1\_F/C1\_R primers using the plasmid p100FA2 as a template, respectively.

Gene deletion and native promoter change from the genomic DNA. Deletion of the ppsR repressor gene and native promoter change of the ppsA gene from the genomic DNA of the DH5α\_GTPS strain were carried out by following the homologous recombination method. The DNA cassette for deletion and promoter change was prepared by two rounds of PCR. The first round of PCR was carried out with the ppsF and ppsR primers using the plasmid pMtrc9 as a template, and the second round of PCR was carried out with the ppsExF and ppsExR primers using the PCR product from the first round of PCR as a template. Later procedures for gene deletion and promoter change were carried out by following the previously reported protocol14. Verification of the ppsR repressor gene deletion and promoter change of the ppsA gene was carried out by colony PCR using ppsVF and ppsVR primers. Hereafter, all of the gene deletions were carried out by following the above-mentioned procedures. Deletion of purT from the genomic DNA of the AKO strain was carried out using a DNA cassette for purT deletion. The DNA cassette for purT deletion was prepared by two-round PCR. The first round of PCR was carried out using purTKOF and purTKOR primers with the plasmid pMloxC as a template and the second round of PCR was carried out using the purTKOExF and purTKOExR primers with the first-round PCR product as a template. Verification of purT deletion was carried out by colony PCR using purTKOVF and purTKOVR primers.

Cultivation conditions. Cells were inoculated into 10 ml LB medium containing appropriate antibiotics (100 μg ml−1 ampicillin or 17 μg ml−1 chloramphenicol) and grown for 12 h. Then, cells were transferred to M9 minimal medium containing 5 g l−1 glucose, 4.43 g l−1 sodium FA (3 g l−1 FA equivalent) and appropriate antibiotics (100 μg ml−1 ampicillin or 17 μg ml−1 chloramphenicol) and grown for

24 h. For the cultivation using $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and FA alone, the precultured cells $( \mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 2–3) were washed once with fresh M9 minimal medium to remove all of the other nutrients, resuspended in 1.5 ml fresh M9 minimal medium and inoculated into a flask (100-ml baffled flask with a working volume of 30 ml, 300-ml baffled flask with a working volume of 50 ml, or 100-ml Erlenmeyer flask with a working volume of 30 ml) containing M9 minimal medium supplemented with 4.43 g l−1 sodium $\mathrm { F A } ( 3 \mathrm { g l } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { F A }$ equivalent) to give an initial $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 } ^ { - } \mathrm { o f } 0 . 0 7 .$ . Cells were cultivated at 200 r.p.m. and $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ in an $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 } / \mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ control orbital shaker (World Science) having a controlled gas composition of 10 mol/mol% of CO , 18 mol/mol% of O and 72 mol/mol% of N . The FA concentration was maintained a $2 - 3 { \bf g } 1 ^ { - 1 }$ throughout the cultivation by adding 1 M sodium FA or 10 v/v% of FA solution.

Bioreactor cultivation. Bioreactor cultures of the FC8 strain were carried out in a 1.3-l Bioflow 110 bioreactor (New Brunswick Scientific) with a working volume of 500 ml. M9 minimal medium supplemented with $4 . 4 3 \mathrm { g l ^ { - 1 } }$ sodium $\mathrm { F A } \ ( 3 \mathrm { g l ^ { - 1 } F A }$ equivalent) was used. Before inoculation to the bioreactor, cells were washed once with fresh M9 minimal medium. The temperature was controlled at 32 °C and an initial agitation speed was set at 500 r.p.m. using a magnetic-drive pitched-blade impeller. For the second bioreactor cultivation, the revolutions per minute was increased by 50 r.p.m. per $1 \mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ unit increase up to 750 r.p.m. During the fed-batch cultivation, FA was fed by pH-stat mode by automatically controlling the pH at 6.8 using 30 v/v% of FA solution. The bioreactor was continuously sparged with a mixture of air and industrial-grade CO at a 9:1 volume ratio at a flow rate of 500 ml min−1 using a flow controller (MKS Instruments).

Colony-forming units and DCW measurement. To measure the number of c.f.u., culture broth was diluted through a serial dilution; 100 µl of culture broth was mixed with 900 µl of fresh LB medium. Next, 100 µl of the culture broth and LB medium mixture was taken and mixed with 900 µl of fresh LB medium. This procedure was repeated 4 to 6 times to make the number of cells per millilitre under 1,000 per millilitre. Fina ${ \mathrm { l y } } ,$ 100 µl of the diluted culture broth was spread on the LB agar plate containing $1 0 0 \dot { \mu } \mathrm { g } \mathrm { m l } \dot { - } 1$ ampicillin or $1 7 \mu \mathrm { g m l ^ { - 1 } }$ chloramphenicol. The LB agar plate was incubated for 24 h at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ The number of colonies on the plate was counted and the number of c.f.u. per millilitre was calculated by multiplying by the dilution factor. To measure DCWs, cell samples (100 ml $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 } \dot { \mathbf { o f } } \sim 1 )$ were collected by centrifugation at 13,000g for 5 min and the supernatant was discarded. The cells were washed with 10 ml deionized water and centrifuged at 13,000g for 5 min, and the supernatant was discarded. The washed cells were frozen at −80 °C for 1 h and freeze-dried for 12 h. Completely dried cells were weighed using a microbalance.

Metabolic flux analysis using 13C-labelled glucose. The isotope analyses of the FC1 and FC2 strains were carried out using the following procedure. Cells were inoculated into 10 ml LB medium containing 100 μg ml−1 ampicillin and grown for 12 h. Then, cells were transferred to M9 minimal medium containing $5 \mathrm { g l ^ { - 1 } }$ glucose, 4.43 g l−1 sodium FA (3 g l−1 FA equivalent) and 100 μg ml−1 ampicillin and grown for 24 h. Next, the cells were inoculated into M9 minimal medium supplemented with 0.1 $\mathrm { g l ^ { - 1 } \left[ U - ^ { 1 3 } C \right] }$ ]glucose, $4 . 4 3 \mathrm { g l } ^ { - 1 }$ sodium FA (3 g l−1 FA equivalent) and 100 μg ml−1 ampicillin. Cells were cultivated using a 100-ml baffled flask with a working volume of 30 ml at 200 r.p.m. and $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ in an $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 } / \mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ control orbital shaker (World Science) having a controlled gas composition of 10 mol/mol% of $\mathrm { C O } _ { \mathfrak { P } } ,$ , 18 mol/mol% o $\mathrm { \dot { \Omega } } _ { \mathrm { \Omega } } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and 72 mol/mol% o $\mathrm { \ddot { N } } _ { 2 } .$ . After 72 h of cultivation, $0 . 1 { \bf g } 1 ^ { - 1 } [ \mathrm { U } . ^ { 1 3 } \bar { \mathrm { C } }$ ]glucose was also added. Cell samples (1 ml $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 } { \bf o f } \sim 3 )$ for $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ isotope analysis were collected after 120 h of flask cultivation. The isotope analyses of the FC5 and FC8 strains were carried out as follows. Cells were inoculated into 10 ml LB medium containing appropriate antibiotics (100 μg ml−1 ampicillin or 17 μg ml−1 chloramphenicol) and grown for 12 h. Next, the cells were transferred to M9 minimal medium supplemented with $5 { \bf g } ^ { 1 ^ { - 1 } } \left[ \mathrm { U } ^ { . 1 3 } \mathrm { C } \right.$ ]glucose, 4.43 g l−1 13C-labelled sodium FA (3 g l−1 FA equivalent), and 100 μg ml−1 ampicillin or $1 7 \mu \mathrm { g } \mathrm { m l } ^ { - 1 }$ chloramphenicol and cultured for 24 h. After that, the precultured cells $\mathrm { \bar { ( O D _ { 6 0 0 } } }$ of 2–3) were inoculated into M9 minimal medium containing $4 . 4 3 \mathrm { g l } ^ { - 1 }$ sodium FA $( 3 \mathrm { g l ^ { - 1 } }$ FA equivalent) to make an initial $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 } { \bf o f } 0 . 0 7$ . Before inoculation, cells were washed once with fresh M9 minimal medium. Cell samples (1 ml $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 } { \bf o f } \sim 3 )$ for $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ isotope analysis were collected after 100 h of flask cultivation. All of the cultivations were carried out in the above-mentioned $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 } / \mathrm { C O } _ { 3 }$ control orbital shaker using a 300-ml baffled flask with a working volume of 50 ml. The collected cells were washed with Tris-HCl (pH 7.6) and hydrolysed with 1 ml 6 M HCl in a dry heating block at 105 °C for 24 h. The hydrolysate was dried at 85 °C in a dry oven. The 12C ratios in proteinogenic amino acids were calculated using the formula below.

$$
\frac { \sum _ { i = 0 } ^ { n } x _ { i } ( n - i ) } { n }
$$

where n is the number of carbons in the amino acids (for example, $n = 2$ for glycine; $n = 3$ for serine and alanine), i is the number of 13C-labelled carbons and X is the ratio of proteinogenic amino acids containing $i ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ carbons.

Microscope image. Culture broth (1 ml) was centrifuged at $_ { 1 3 , 0 0 0 g }$ for 1 min and the supernatant was discarded. The cells were washed with 1 ml deionized water and centrifuged at 13,000g for 1 min and 950 µl of supernatant was discarded. Pellets and the remaining supernatant were mixed by pipetting, and 10 µl of the mixture was

spotted on a glass microscope slide (Paul Marienfeld) and covered with a 0.17-mm microscope cover glass (Paul Marienfeld). Immersion oil (10 μl) for microscopy (Merck) was spotted onto the microscope cover glass. Microscopic images were obtained using a Nikon OPTIPHOT-2 microscope (Nikon) at ×1,000 magnification.

mRNA quantification using real-time PCR. The mRNA expression levels of the ppsA, gcvT, cyoA, cyoB, cydA and cydB genes were quantified by the following procedure. Cells were cultured following the cultivation method described above. Cells (1 ml $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 } { \bf o f } \sim 1 )$ were collected after 100 h of cultivation. Total RNA was extracted using the RNA Extraction Kit (Intron Biotechnology). Real-time PCR (rtPCR) was carried out using the LightCycler96 (Roche) RT-PCR machine and One Step SYBR PrimeScript RT-PCR Kit (Takara) following the manufacturers’ protocols. Primers used for rtPCR were designed using the Primer3 software (http://bioinfo.ut.ee/primer3-0.4.0/). RNA quantification was performed using a ΔΔ cycle threshold (Ct) method with rrsA as a reference gene. The rtPCR results were analysed using LightCycler96 software (Roche).

Analytical procedures. To measure FA and glucose concentrations, the culture broth was centrifuged at 13,000g for 10min and the supernatant was collected and filtered using a cellulose acetate membrane filter (pore size of 0.22µm; Millipore). Prepared samples were injected into a high-performance liquid chromatography instrument (Waters 1515/2414/2707) equipped with a packed column (Metacarb 87H; MetaChem Technologies) and a refractive index detector (RI-27; Shodex) to measure FA concentration. Cell growth was monitored a $\tan _ { 6 0 0 }$ using an Ultrospec 3000 spectrophotometer (Pharmacia Biotech). $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ isotope analysis using dried amino-acid hydrolysates was carried out by the following procedure. The dried amino-acid hydrolysate was derivatized with 50μl of dimethylformamide and 50μl of N-(ter t-butyldimethylsilyl)-N-methyl-trifluoroacetamide at 85 °C for 1 h. The derivatized amino-acid hydrolysate was analysed using a 6890 gas chromatograph system (Agilent Technologies) combined with a 5875 Inert XL mass spectrometry system (Agilent Technologies). Gas chromatography–mass spectrometry operation and data analysis were carried out following the protocol described in our previous study9.

paragraphs.text: Junho Bang  1,2, Chang Hun Hwang  1,2, Jung Ho Ahn1,2, Jong An Lee1,2 and Sang Yup Lee  1,2,3<sup> ✉</sup>

We engineered Escherichia coli to grow on $\mathbf { c o } _ { 2 }$ and formic acid alone by introducing the synthetic $\mathbf { c o } _ { 2 }$ and formic acid assimilation pathway, expressing two formate dehydrogenase genes, fine-tuning metabolic fluxes and optimizing the levels of cytochrome bo and bd-I ubiquinol oxidase. Our engineered strain can grow to an optical density at 600 nm of 7.38 in 450 h, and shows promise as a platform strain growing on $\mathbf { c o } _ { 2 }$ and formic acid alone.

Biological conversion of $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ into useful compounds could enable production of value-added products from CO (ref. 1). To efficiently assimilate $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 } ,$ the combined use of $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and formic acid (FA), which is produced by liquefaction of $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ by a chemical reaction, has been suggested $2 - { 5 }$ FA can be readily produced from $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ (ref. 6), and is easy to store and transport7. FA can be assimilated more efficiently than $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ by microorganisms8 and can be converted into reducing power by formate dehydrogenase (Fdh). Owing to these advantages, development of a synthetic microorganism capable of growing on $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and FA alone has been pursued. Recently, limited growth of Escherichia coli strains on $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and FA has been reported9–11 (Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Note 2). However, the final optical densities at 600 nm $\left( \mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 } \right)$ reached by these engineered E. coli strains was low (up to $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 1). Development of an E. coli strain that can efficiently grow to a higher cell density on $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and FA alone is needed for industrial biotechnology applications.

We engineered an E. coli strain capable of growing on CO and FA alone (Fig. 1a). First, strain FC1 was constructed by introducing a reconstructed tetrahydrofolate (THF) cycle, reverse glycine cleavage reaction and Candida boidinii Fdh (CbFdh) into the E. coli DH5α\_ GTPS strain (a strain with the gcvR, pflB and serA genes deleted and the native promoter of gcvT replaced with trc; Supplementary Note 3, Extended Data Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 2). However, FC1 failed to grow on CO and FA alone (Fig. 1b).

We hypothesized that insufficient gluconeogenesis, simultaneous expression of the purT and ftl genes, and inefficient NADPH supply might be the reasons for the inability of the FC1 strain to grow solely on CO and FA. We solved all three potential problems in turn, resulting in strains FC2 (ppsA overexpression and ppsR deletion in FC1), FC3 (purT deletion in FC2) and FC5 (FC3 strain harbouring p100FA2, which additionally expresses the Arabidopsis thaliana $f d h _ { \mathrm { m u t } }$ gene for NADPH generation from FA; Supplementary Table 2, Supplementary Note 4 and Extended Data Figs. 1b and 2a–d). FC5 grew on $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and FA alone (Fig. 1b and Extended Data Fig. 3a) to an $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 0.285 (0.0633 g dry cell weight (DCW) l−1) in 150 h from an initial $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 0.051 (0.0169 g DCW l−1), showing about 2.5 cell doublings; also, the number of colony-forming units (c.f.u.)

was increased (Extended Data Fig. 3b). Assimilation of $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and FA was confirmed by 13C isotope analysis (Extended Data Fig. 4 and Supplementary Note 5). These results suggest that FC5 can grow on CO and FA alone with active cell division. Next, optimization of isopropyl-β-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG) concentration and aeration conditions enabled cells to grow to a higher density. As a result, the FC5 strain grew to a higher $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 0.533 (from the initial $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 0.07) in 200 h in optimized conditions, which was 0.87-fold higher than that $\left( \mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 } \right)$ of 0.285) obtained earlier (Supplementary Note 6 and Extended Data Fig. 5a–c).

We then optimized plasmid gene expression levels because excessive gene expression might negatively affect cell growth during limited nutrient supply, especially in a medium containing CO and FA alone. Plasmid gene expression levels were fine-tuned by using plasmids with lower copy numbers in FC5 (Fig. 1c) to yield strains FC7 and FC8 (Supplementary Note 7 and Supplementary Table 2), which harboured medium- and low-copy-number plasmids, respectively. The FC8 strain grew up to an $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 0.607 (from the initial $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 0.06) in 200 h solely on $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and FA, 0.14-fold higher than that $( \mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 0.533) of the FC5 strain, while the FC7 strain grew to an $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 0.452, slightly lower than that of the FC5 strain (Fig. 1d). The $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and FA assimilation fluxes and the amount of FA consumed by FC8 were higher than in FC5 (Extended Data Fig. 6a,b), suggesting that in FC5 the plasmid gene expression levels were higher than those actually needed for cell growth on $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and FA (Supplementary Note 7). To demonstrate that the FC8 strain was able to grow to a higher cell density solely on $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and FA, it was cultured using a higher initial inoculum level $( \mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 0.35). The FC8 strain grew to an $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 1.24 (0.343 g DCW l−1) in 100 h (Fig. 2a). Cells were found to be filamented (Fig. 2b), which seems to be one of the reasons for no further growth beyond the $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 1.24 as cell filamentation negatively affects cell growth12.

We hypothesized that cell filamentation might be due to energy deficiency in the cells when growing on CO and FA alone. One way of solving energy deficiency is to more efficiently convert reducing power to ATP. Reducing the cultivation temperature (for example, 28 and $3 3 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ can improve energy efficiency by increasing the expression level of cytochrome bo ubiquinol oxidase (Cyo) while decreasing the expression level of cytochrome bd-I ubiquinol oxidase (Cyd; Fig. 2c and Supplementary Note 8). We monitored growth of FC8 at 30, 32 and ${ \bar { 3 } } { \bar { 3 } } ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ . The highest level of cell growth was observed at $3 2 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ (see Supplementary Note 9 and Extended Data Fig. 7a–c for detailed results); the FC8 strain grew from an initial $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 0.31 to an $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 2.48 (0.687 g DCW l−1) in 244 h (Fig. 2d), consuming 0.41 g FA (for example, $8 . 2 \mathrm { g l } ^ { - 1 }$ FA equivalent). We found that the messenger RNA levels of the cyoAB and cydAB genes, which encode Cyo and Cyd, respectively, were changed as intended at $3 2 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ compared with those at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ (Extended Data Fig. 7d). The biomass yields on FA were $0 . 0 5 5 2 { \scriptstyle \pm 0 . 0 0 0 9 }$ and 0.0365 ± 0.0026 g DCW g−1 FA when the FC8 strain was cultured at 32 and $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { { C } } ,$ respectively (Fig. 2e), suggesting that increasing the Cyo level and decreasing the Cyd level enhanced energy efficiency when growing solely on CO and FA. Thus, cell filamentation was suppressed (Fig. 2b) by more efficiently converting reducing power to ATP.

We cultivated our optimized FC8 strain in a flask starting with a low initial $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 0.018 to examine the maximum number of cell doublings. FC8 grew to an $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 3.59 (0.994 g DCW l−1) in 791.5 h, consuming 0.94 g FA (for example, $1 8 . 8 \mathrm { g l ^ { - 1 } }$ FA equivalent; Fig. 2f), showing 7.64 doublings. As cells grew, the specific growth rate decreased, and consequently the doubling time increased; the specific growth rates at the initial and final time points were 0.0105 and $0 . 0 0 \bar { 2 } 8 \mathrm { h } ^ { - 1 }$ , respectively, while the doubling times were 65.9 and 250.6 h, respectively (Extended Data Fig. 8a).

To determine the maximum achievable $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 } ,$ a bioreactor culture of FC8 starting with a high initial $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 1.02 was analysed. FC8 grew to a maximum $\mathrm { \ O D } _ { 6 0 0 } ^ { - }$ of 7.38 (2.044 g DCW l−1) from an initial $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 1.02 in $4 5 0 \mathrm { h } ,$ consuming 18.2 g FA (for example, $3 6 . 4 \mathrm { g l ^ { - 1 } }$ FA equivalent; Fig. 2g). Three additional bioreactor cultures were independently performed to examine reproducibility, resulting in the maximum $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 7.88 (2.074 g DCW l−1) from an initial $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 1.15 in 412 h, 8.01 (2.29 g DCW l−1) from an initial $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 1.06 in 412 h, and 11.1 (3.466 g DCW l−1) from an initial $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 0.91 in 577 h, respectively (more detailed results are presented in Supplementary Note 10 and Extended Data Fig. 8b–f); thus, the FC8 strain was able to grow to an $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 7–11 from the initial $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of about 1.

In summary, we engineered an E. coli strain capable of growing on $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and FA alone to a higher cell density than previously reported strains. Our work could enable bio-based production of chemicals solely from $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and FA in future (Supplementary Discussion). Although we developed an engineered strain capable of growing to a higher cell density, the low specific growth rate still needs to be improved. This might be achievable using adaptive laboratory evolution of FC8, further metabolic engineering to increase $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 } / \mathrm { \dot { F } A }$ assimilation and energy generation, and/or optimization of bioreactor cultivation conditions.

Bacterial strains and medium composition. The E. coli strains and plasmids used in this study are listed in Supplementary Table 2. Plasmid construction. Plasmid p100FA1 construction was carried out as follows. The DNA fragment of plasmid backbone was prepared by PCR with 100\_F/ mtd\_R primers using the plasmid p100THF as a template. The DNA fragment of FDHcbo was prepared by PCR with FDHcbo\_F/FDHcbo\_R primers using genomic DNA of C. boidinii as a template. Next, the purified DNA fragments of the plasmid backbone and FDHcbo were ligated by a Gibson assembly reaction following the standard protocol13. Finally, the DNA sequence of the constructed plasmid p100FA1 was confirmed by DNA sequencing. Hereafter, all of the plasmid construction procedures were carried out by following the method described above. The plasmid p100FA2 was constructed by a Gibson assembly reaction using the DNA fragments of plasmid backbone and FDHatmut. These DNA fragments were prepared by PCR with 100\_F/FDHcbo\_R1 primers using p100FA1 as a template and FDHat\_F/FDHat\_R primers using the synthesized FDHatmut DNA fragment as a template, respectively. The plasmid p184FA was constructed by a Gibson assembly reaction using the DNA fragments of plasmid backbone and C1\_OPR. These DNA fragments were prepared by PCR with 184\_F/184\_R primers using pACYC184 as a template and with C1\_F/C1\_R primers using the plasmid p100FA2 as a template, respectively. The plasmid p518FA was constructed by a Gibson assembly reaction using the DNA fragments of plasmid backbone and C1\_OPR. These DNA fragments were prepared by PCR with 518\_F/518\_R primers using pJH518 as a template and with C1\_F/C1\_R primers using the plasmid p100FA2 as a template, respectively.

Gene deletion and native promoter change from the genomic DNA. Deletion of the ppsR repressor gene and native promoter change of the ppsA gene from the genomic DNA of the DH5α\_GTPS strain were carried out by following the homologous recombination method. The DNA cassette for deletion and promoter change was prepared by two rounds of PCR. The first round of PCR was carried out with the ppsF and ppsR primers using the plasmid pMtrc9 as a template, and the second round of PCR was carried out with the ppsExF and ppsExR primers using the PCR product from the first round of PCR as a template. Later procedures for gene deletion and promoter change were carried out by following the previously reported protocol14. Verification of the ppsR repressor gene deletion and promoter change of the ppsA gene was carried out by colony PCR using ppsVF and ppsVR primers. Hereafter, all of the gene deletions were carried out by following the above-mentioned procedures. Deletion of purT from the genomic DNA of the AKO strain was carried out using a DNA cassette for purT deletion. The DNA cassette for purT deletion was prepared by two-round PCR. The first round of PCR was carried out using purTKOF and purTKOR primers with the plasmid pMloxC as a template and the second round of PCR was carried out using the purTKOExF and purTKOExR primers with the first-round PCR product as a template. Verification of purT deletion was carried out by colony PCR using purTKOVF and purTKOVR primers.

Cultivation conditions. Cells were inoculated into 10 ml LB medium containing appropriate antibiotics (100 μg ml−1 ampicillin or 17 μg ml−1 chloramphenicol) and grown for 12 h. Then, cells were transferred to M9 minimal medium containing 5 g l−1 glucose, 4.43 g l−1 sodium FA (3 g l−1 FA equivalent) and appropriate antibiotics (100 μg ml−1 ampicillin or 17 μg ml−1 chloramphenicol) and grown for

24 h. For the cultivation using $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and FA alone, the precultured cells $( \mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 2–3) were washed once with fresh M9 minimal medium to remove all of the other nutrients, resuspended in 1.5 ml fresh M9 minimal medium and inoculated into a flask (100-ml baffled flask with a working volume of 30 ml, 300-ml baffled flask with a working volume of 50 ml, or 100-ml Erlenmeyer flask with a working volume of 30 ml) containing M9 minimal medium supplemented with 4.43 g l−1 sodium $\mathrm { F A } ( 3 \mathrm { g l } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { F A }$ equivalent) to give an initial $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 } ^ { - } \mathrm { o f } 0 . 0 7 .$ . Cells were cultivated at 200 r.p.m. and $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ in an $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 } / \mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ control orbital shaker (World Science) having a controlled gas composition of 10 mol/mol% of CO , 18 mol/mol% of O and 72 mol/mol% of N . The FA concentration was maintained a $2 - 3 { \bf g } 1 ^ { - 1 }$ throughout the cultivation by adding 1 M sodium FA or 10 v/v% of FA solution.

Bioreactor cultivation. Bioreactor cultures of the FC8 strain were carried out in a 1.3-l Bioflow 110 bioreactor (New Brunswick Scientific) with a working volume of 500 ml. M9 minimal medium supplemented with $4 . 4 3 \mathrm { g l ^ { - 1 } }$ sodium $\mathrm { F A } \ ( 3 \mathrm { g l ^ { - 1 } F A }$ equivalent) was used. Before inoculation to the bioreactor, cells were washed once with fresh M9 minimal medium. The temperature was controlled at 32 °C and an initial agitation speed was set at 500 r.p.m. using a magnetic-drive pitched-blade impeller. For the second bioreactor cultivation, the revolutions per minute was increased by 50 r.p.m. per $1 \mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ unit increase up to 750 r.p.m. During the fed-batch cultivation, FA was fed by pH-stat mode by automatically controlling the pH at 6.8 using 30 v/v% of FA solution. The bioreactor was continuously sparged with a mixture of air and industrial-grade CO at a 9:1 volume ratio at a flow rate of 500 ml min−1 using a flow controller (MKS Instruments).

Colony-forming units and DCW measurement. To measure the number of c.f.u., culture broth was diluted through a serial dilution; 100 µl of culture broth was mixed with 900 µl of fresh LB medium. Next, 100 µl of the culture broth and LB medium mixture was taken and mixed with 900 µl of fresh LB medium. This procedure was repeated 4 to 6 times to make the number of cells per millilitre under 1,000 per millilitre. Fina ${ \mathrm { l y } } ,$ 100 µl of the diluted culture broth was spread on the LB agar plate containing $1 0 0 \dot { \mu } \mathrm { g } \mathrm { m l } \dot { - } 1$ ampicillin or $1 7 \mu \mathrm { g m l ^ { - 1 } }$ chloramphenicol. The LB agar plate was incubated for 24 h at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ The number of colonies on the plate was counted and the number of c.f.u. per millilitre was calculated by multiplying by the dilution factor. To measure DCWs, cell samples (100 ml $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 } \dot { \mathbf { o f } } \sim 1 )$ were collected by centrifugation at 13,000g for 5 min and the supernatant was discarded. The cells were washed with 10 ml deionized water and centrifuged at 13,000g for 5 min, and the supernatant was discarded. The washed cells were frozen at −80 °C for 1 h and freeze-dried for 12 h. Completely dried cells were weighed using a microbalance.

mRNA quantification using real-time PCR. The mRNA expression levels of the ppsA, gcvT, cyoA, cyoB, cydA and cydB genes were quantified by the following procedure. Cells were cultured following the cultivation method described above. Cells (1 ml $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 } { \bf o f } \sim 1 )$ were collected after 100 h of cultivation. Total RNA was extracted using the RNA Extraction Kit (Intron Biotechnology). Real-time PCR (rtPCR) was carried out using the LightCycler96 (Roche) RT-PCR machine and One Step SYBR PrimeScript RT-PCR Kit (Takara) following the manufacturers’ protocols. Primers used for rtPCR were designed using the Primer3 software (http://bioinfo.ut.ee/primer3-0.4.0/). RNA quantification was performed using a ΔΔ cycle threshold (Ct) method with rrsA as a reference gene. The rtPCR results were analysed using LightCycler96 software (Roche).

Analytical procedures. To measure FA and glucose concentrations, the culture broth was centrifuged at 13,000g for 10min and the supernatant was collected and filtered using a cellulose acetate membrane filter (pore size of 0.22µm; Millipore). Prepared samples were injected into a high-performance liquid chromatography instrument (Waters 1515/2414/2707) equipped with a packed column (Metacarb 87H; MetaChem Technologies) and a refractive index detector (RI-27; Shodex) to measure FA concentration. Cell growth was monitored a $\tan _ { 6 0 0 }$ using an Ultrospec 3000 spectrophotometer (Pharmacia Biotech). $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ isotope analysis using dried amino-acid hydrolysates was carried out by the following procedure. The dried amino-acid hydrolysate was derivatized with 50μl of dimethylformamide and 50μl of N-(ter t-butyldimethylsilyl)-N-methyl-trifluoroacetamide at 85 °C for 1 h. The derivatized amino-acid hydrolysate was analysed using a 6890 gas chromatograph system (Agilent Technologies) combined with a 5875 Inert XL mass spectrometry system (Agilent Technologies). Gas chromatography–mass spectrometry operation and data analysis were carried out following the protocol described in our previous study9.
